claims.text: As-received Q235 steel has a naturally formed, thin, adherent iron oxide/hydroxide surface layer.
The native surface oxide gives Q235 steel moderate corrosion protection at room temperature.
At room temperature, the native oxide on Q235 steel is compact and self-healing.
Exposure at 700–900 °C in aggressive molten salt increases atomic mobility and grain-boundary diffusion in Q235 steel or its oxide scale.
Enhanced diffusion and thermal effects accelerate growth of the Q235 surface oxide.
High-temperature molten-salt exposure transforms the native oxide into a thick, porous, and poorly adherent iron oxide scale.
Thermal stresses cause the high-temperature oxide scale to spall.
Oxide-scale spallation exposes fresh Q235 steel to the corrosive environment.
Exposure of fresh metal after scale failure leads to rapid oxidation.
Molten salt drives dissolution of exposed alloy constituents.
Relative to room-temperature salt contact, Q235 steel exposed to molten salt at 700–900 °C will exhibit significantly greater mass loss.
Relative to the room-temperature control, high-temperature samples will have a thicker, more porous, more spalled, and less adherent oxide scale.
High-temperature samples will exhibit more aggressive corrosion attack on the underlying Q235 substrate than the room-temperature control.
The proposed degradation mechanism applies when the native oxide is the sole protection and the salt is molten at high temperature.
Additional alloying or protective coatings may change or suppress the proposed oxide-failure mechanism.
The controlled study will compare nominally identical Q235 samples exposed to Na2SO4/NaCl at 700–900 °C with samples held in contact with the same salt composition at room temperature.
Mass change, scale thickness, porosity, phase composition, and adhesion will be measured by gravimetry, SEM, XRD, and mechanical adhesion testing.
Absence of increased mass loss and of thicker, more porous, spalled, or poorly adherent oxide at high temperature relative to the room-temperature control would falsify the hypothesis.
